research_question: Can positive views of aging help older adults maintain or improve their cognitive functioning and mobility?
explanation: Exposure — Positive age beliefs: Baseline score on the five-item Attitude Toward Aging subscale of the Philadelphia Geriatric Center Morale Scale. Responses range from strongly disagree to strongly agree; negative items are reverse-scored. Total scores range from 5 to 30, with higher scores indicating more-positive age beliefs. The participant’s first age-belief wave, administered to one random half of the HRS sample in 2008 and the other half in 2010, was used as baseline. The primary models used the score as a predictor; a median split was used only for Figure 1. || Outcome — Physical improvement in walking speed: Change in walking speed from baseline to the participant’s last follow-up wave, up to 12 years later. HRS walking speed was assessed by asking participants to walk at normal speed, using walking devices if helpful, over 8.21 feet / 2.5 meters, with two trials at baseline and follow-up waves. Speed was calculated as distance divided by time; the analysis used the faster of the two trials to assess maximum capability. Baseline walking speed was reported in cm/s. For the primary binary outcome, participants were coded 1 if last-follow-up walking speed exceeded baseline walking speed and 0 if they stayed the same or walked slower. || Outcome — Cognitive improvement: Change in 27-point Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (TICS) global cognition score from baseline to the participant’s last follow-up wave, up to 12 years later. The paper subtracted baseline TICS from last-follow-up TICS; larger values indicate improvement. For the primary binary outcome, participants were coded 1 if the difference was above 0 and 0 if cognition stayed the same or declined.
source_paper_title: Aging Redefined: Cognitive and Physical Improvement with Positive Age Beliefs

explanation: Exposure — Sarcopenia index based on serum creatinine and cystatin C: Primary exposure measured at the 2016 HRS wave from venous blood biomarkers. Analyses treated SI both continuously per 1-SD increase and categorically in quartiles, with the lowest quartile as reference. || Outcome — Osteoarthritis status: prevalent and incident self-reported doctor-diagnosed OA: Outcome was self-reported osteoarthritis. Incident OA was defined among participants free of OA at baseline as a new OA diagnosis reported during follow-up from the 2016 interview through the 2020 wave.

research_question: Could long-term patterns of depressive symptoms be connected to chronic lung disease and function in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Depressive symptom trajectory based on overall CESD-8 depressive symptoms: For HRS, depressive symptoms were measured at Wave 5, Wave 6, and Wave 7 using the 8-item CESD, with eight binary yes/no past-week symptom items summed to a total score from 0 to 8. Overall elevated depressive symptoms were defined as CESD-8 score ≥3 at each wave. Five trajectory categories over the three waves were predefined from whether symptoms were elevated over time: consistently low, decreasing, fluctuating, increasing, and consistently high. || Outcome — Incident chronic lung diseases: Incident CLDs in HRS were identified during follow-up after the depressive-symptom trajectory exposure period, from Wave 8 through Wave 12, using self-reported physician diagnoses. The CLD definition included chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and other pulmonary diseases, while excluding asthma and lung cancer. Time-to-event follow-up ended at first CLD occurrence or censoring. || Outcome — Peak expiratory flow lung function: Lung function in HRS was assessed at Wave 8 using peak expiratory flow. Trained technicians measured PEF with a peak flow meter. Participants stood upright, took a deep breath, and blew into the meter as forcefully and quickly as possible three times; the maximum of the three PEF values was used for analysis. The paper does not state the measurement unit in the supplied text.
source_paper_title: Association between depressive symptom and respiratory health in two prospective cohort studies.

research_question: How might race and ethnicity shape cognitive aging and dementia risk?

Respondents subtracted 7 from 100 five times, earning one point for each correct answer, for a per-wave score from 0 to 5; descriptive results indicate the study summed this score across 2012–2020 waves, giving a possible range of 0 to 25. || Exposure — Attention and processing speed score from backward counting: Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status-27 backward counting task used to measure attention and processing speed. Respondents counted backward continuously from 20 to 10 twice; each correct trial was worth one point, for a per-wave score from 0 to 2. Descriptive results indicate the study summed this score across 2012–2020 waves, giving a possible range of 0 to 10.
source_paper_title: Association of diabetes risk with changes in memory, working memory, and processing speed among older adults.

research_question: How might childhood socioeconomic conditions shape college completion later in life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Retrospective childhood SES measured in the HRS Demographics module at the respondent’s first HRS interview. Includes respondent reports of father’s highest grade completed and mother’s highest grade completed, analyzed continuously in some analyses and categorically as less than 8 years, 8–11 years, and 12 or more years; and respondent report of family financial status while growing up from birth to age 16, categorized as pretty well-off, about average, or poor. || Outcome — Respondent’s own college degree attainment: Respondent’s own years of schooling reported in the baseline HRS survey, recoded for predictive-validity analyses as a binary indicator of having 16 or more years of education versus fewer than 16 years, interpreted as 4-year college degree attainment. || Exposure — Respondent’s own adult educational attainment categories: Respondent’s own baseline HRS educational attainment modeled categorically in analyses estimating education differences in later-life outcomes: less than 12 years, 12 years, 13–15 years, and 16 or more years.
source_paper_title: The Validity and Reliability of Retrospective Measures of Childhood Socioeconomic Status in the Health and Retirement Study: Evidence from the 1940 U.S. Census.

research_question: How might persistent hearing or vision problems affect depression in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Cumulative hearing loss: Self-rated hearing was measured in each HRS wave from 1998 through 2006. Respondents rating their hearing as fair or poor, using a hearing aid as usual, were classified as having hearing loss for that wave; excellent, very good, or good were classified as no hearing loss. Cumulative hearing loss was the count of waves with hearing loss across the five exposure waves, ranging from 0 to 5, and was also categorized as never, 1 time point, 2 time points, or ≥3 time points. || Exposure — Cumulative vision loss: Vision was measured in each HRS wave from 1998 through 2006 using self-rated overall eyesight, distance vision, and near vision, using glasses or corrective lenses as usual. If any of the three vision ratings was fair, poor, or legally blind, the respondent was classified as having vision loss for that wave; other responses were classified as no vision loss. Cumulative vision loss was counted across the five exposure waves, using the same frequency approach as cumulative hearing loss, and was also categorized as never, 1 time point, 2 time points, or ≥3 time points. || Exposure — Cumulative dual sensory loss: For each HRS wave from 1998 through 2006, dual sensory loss was defined as having both wave-specific hearing loss and wave-specific vision loss in the same wave. Cumulative dual sensory loss was the count of waves with dual sensory loss across the five exposure waves, ranging from 0 to 5, and was analyzed continuously and categorically as never, 1 time point, 2 time points, or ≥3 time points. || Exposure — Cumulative any sensory loss: For each HRS wave from 1998 through 2006, any sensory loss was defined as having either wave-specific vision loss or wave-specific hearing loss in the same wave. The paper reports cumulative any sensory loss as a continuous index ranging from 0 to 10 and as categories of never, 1 time point, 2 time points, or ≥3 time points. || Outcome — Depressive symptom trajectory: Depressive symptoms were measured repeatedly from HRS 2008 through 2020 using the 8-item short Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale. Each item was scored 0 for symptom absent or 1 for symptom present, producing a total score from 0 to 8, with higher scores indicating more severe depressive symptoms. Longitudinal analyses modeled change in CES-D scores over follow-up. || Outcome — Incident depression: Depression was defined as an 8-item CES-D total score of 3 or higher. For incident depression analyses, participants with prevalent depression at the 2008 baseline were excluded, and new depression was assessed during follow-up from 2008 through 2020.
source_paper_title: Associations of cumulative hearing and vision loss with depression among U.S. adults aged 50 and older: results from the health and retirement study.

research_question: Could vitamin D help connect personality with memory in later life?
hrs_column_ids: PVD2; PVD3; QD174; QD184; QD174W; QD184W
explanation: Mediator measurements: In HRS, vitamin D was measured from blood collected in the 2016 Venous Blood Study. Assays used liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry at the University of Michigan Advanced Research and Diagnostic Laboratory. Vitamin D was measured separately as Vitamin D2 and Vitamin D3 in ng/mL; both were natural-log transformed and entered simultaneously as mediators in the HRS analyses. || Outcome measurements: Follow-up memory in HRS 2018 was assessed with immediate and delayed recall tasks. Participants heard/read a list of 10 common words and recalled as many as possible immediately and after about a 5-minute delay. The number of correctly recalled words across the immediate and delayed trials was summed to form a total memory score ranging from 0 to 20 words.
source_paper_title: The mediating role of Vitamin D in the association between personality and memory: Evidence from two samples.

research_question: How might functional disability shape vulnerability to COVID-19 and its consequences among older adults, and what role might vaccination play?
explanation: Exposure — Baseline functional disability: Binary indicator measured at baseline in 2018. Respondents were classified as having functional disability if they reported any difficulty with at least one activity of daily living or instrumental activity of daily living. Responses of “yes” or “don’t do due to a health or memory problem” counted as difficulty; “no” counted as no difficulty. || Outcome — COVID-19 outcomes: Self-reported COVID-19 outcomes from the 2021 HRS Perspectives on the Pandemic Mail-in Survey. Primary outcome was COVID-19 infection. Secondary outcomes among infected respondents included emergency room use because of the virus, hospital admission because of the virus, length of hospital stay measured as number of nights, and post-COVID conditions defined as lingering physical or mental health effects from the virus. For binary outcomes, “yes” or “probably yes (I think so)” counted as positive; “no” or “probably no (I don’t think so)” counted as negative. || Mediator — COVID-19 vaccination status: Vaccination status from the 2021 Pandemic Survey. Respondents were classified as vaccinated if they reported having had two shots, having had one shot and waiting for the second, or having had one shot and not needing a second. Respondents were classified as not vaccinated if they reported having an appointment soon or no vaccination. Blank or multiple responses were treated as missing in the paper. The same measure was also used for vaccination-stratified analyses.
source_paper_title: Association of disability with COVID-19 outcomes in older adults: a prospective analysis of the US health and retirement study.

research_question: How well do dementia classifications work across racial and ethnic groups in later life?
explanation: Outcome — HCAP cognitive status / dementia classification: Target-data criterion outcome from the 2016 HRS-HCAP in-depth cognitive assessment. Participants were assigned to one of three cognitive-status categories—normal cognition, cognitive impairment, or dementia—and the transfer-learning models were evaluated for estimating prevalent dementia status against this HCAP classification. || Moderator — Race and ethnicity group: Participants were grouped as non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, or Hispanic for eligibility/stratification and for evaluating group-specific model performance. Participants missing race/ethnicity information or identifying outside these three groups were excluded from the analytic samples.
source_paper_title: Improving accuracy in the estimation of probable dementia in racially and ethnically diverse groups with penalized regression and transfer learning.

research_question: How might pre-pandemic functional or cognitive impairment shape the later consequences of COVID-19 for older adults?
explanation: Exposure — COVID-19 infection history: Self-reported history of COVID-19 infection, identified from either the 2020 HRS survey or the 2021 Spring/Fall Perspectives on the Pandemic HRS survey. || Moderator — Baseline functional limitation status: 2018 Functional Limitation score summing difficulty across 12 physical-function tasks. Each item with no difficulty was scored 0 and any difficulty was scored 1, producing a 0–12 score categorized as less limitations 0–2, moderate limitations 3–7, and most limitations 8–12. || Moderator — Baseline cognitive status: 2018 cognitive status categorized as normal, cognitive impairment-no dementia, or dementia. For self-respondents, the Crimmins 27-point cognitive scale used immediate and delayed 10-noun recall, serial 7 subtraction, and backward count from 20, with cut points normal 12–27, CIND 7–11, and dementia 0–6. For proxy respondents, an 11-point Langa scale used proxy memory rating, limitations in 5 IADLs, and interviewer assessment of cognitive difficulty, with cut points normal 0–2, CIND 3–5, and dementia 6–11. || Outcome — Health services use: 2022 HRS self-report indicators of whether the respondent had a nursing home stay, had a hospitalization, or saw a doctor in the last two years. || Outcome — Work-related outcomes: 2022 HRS indicators of whether the respondent was able to work, had a work-limiting impairment, or had applied for disability benefits through SSI and/or SSDI.
source_paper_title: Health service use and work related outcomes in older adults with functional and cognitive impairments during the COVID-19 pandemic.

research_question: Could body shape help predict cancer risk in later life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Baseline body roundness index (BRI) calculated from measured standing height in meters and waist circumference in centimeters using the Thomas et al. formula. The baseline wave was each participant’s earliest eligible wave with available BRI data. The paper modeled BRI nonlinearly, then categorized participants using an RCS-derived cutoff at BRI = 5.06, primarily comparing BRI ≤ 5.06 versus BRI > 5.06; it also used four BRI groups split at 5.06 and within-category medians. || Outcome — Incident cancer diagnosis: Overall cancer incidence during follow-up, based on a binary yes/no self-reported physician-confirmed cancer diagnosis. Participants with cancer before baseline were excluded. For incident cases, because exact diagnosis date was unavailable, diagnosis time was estimated as the midpoint between the first wave reporting cancer and the last wave without a cancer diagnosis; noncases were followed to their last recorded study wave.
source_paper_title: Association Between Body Roundness Index and Cancer Risk, With Further Stratification by Cardiometabolic Disease Status: Findings From Three National Longitudinal Cohorts.

research_question: How do long-term pain trajectories differ by gender in later life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Repeated self-reported pain severity was coded as a 0–3 pain index at HRS interviews: no frequent pain = 0; if often troubled by pain, usual pain intensity mild = 1, moderate = 2, severe = 3. Latent class mixed models using a cubic polynomial were used to classify longitudinal pain-score patterns into three trajectory classes, labeled Fluctuation, Low-level, and High-level, with sex-stratified trajectory solutions also reported. || Exposure measurements: Individual-level fluctuation in repeated pain scores was quantified using Variability Independent of the Mean (VIM), intended to capture pain-amplitude variability independent of average pain level. Higher VIM represented greater pain variability. The paper does not provide the exact VIM formula, exponent, or required number/timing of pain observations. || Moderator — Sex: Participant sex was recorded as male or female and used for sex-stratified analyses and testing of sex-specific pain associations with cognition and depressive symptoms.
source_paper_title: Sex-specific trajectories and variability of pain burden in relation to cognitive decline and depressive symptoms in older adults: a prospective cohort study from health and retirement study.

research_question: Could physical activity be linked to longevity in later life?
explanation: Moderator measurements: Baseline leisure-time physical activity in HRS was assessed by questionnaire items on vigorous, moderate, and light activity frequency. Frequency responses were assigned intensity-specific values and summed into a physical activity index score from 0 to 18: vigorous activity values 0, 2, 6, and 12; moderate activity values 0, 1, 3, and 6; light activity values 0, 0.5, 1.5, and 3 for the respective frequency categories. An index score ≥9 was classified as regular activity meeting or exceeding WHO physical activity recommendations; lower scores were classified as inactivity. || Outcome measurements: Mortality during follow-up was ascertained from HRS mortality sources, including trace data, National Death Index linkage, registry or Medicare claims sources, and exit interviews with proxy respondents. The analysis used death status and time-to-event/person-years during follow-up.
source_paper_title: Interaction between physical activity and deficit-based frailty on all-cause mortality in older adults: a prospective study of five population-based cohorts.

research_question: Could respiratory sarcopenia help predict survival among older adults with chronic kidney disease?

explanation: Exposure — Respiratory sarcopenia status and longitudinal transition: Respiratory sarcopenia was defined as the co-occurrence of low respiratory muscle strength and low muscle mass. research_question: How might prior incarceration shape cognitive aging?

explanation: Exposure — Prior incarceration: Binary indicator of whether the respondent had ever been incarcerated, measured from the 2012 or 2014 HRS leave-behind questionnaire. The Langa-Weir cognition measure is a 27-point scale, with higher scores indicating better cognitive functioning. Group-based trajectory modeling assigned each respondent to the trajectory group with the highest posterior probability. The selected model had four trajectory groups: lowest and continuously declining cognition; moderate-low cognition that declined rapidly after the mid-70s; higher cognition that was stable then declined more slowly; and highest/stable cognition.

research_question: Could avoiding prescription sleep medicines reduce fall-related injuries in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Regular prescription sleep medication use: Prevalent regular use of prescription medication to help sleep among 2016 HRS respondents. The simulation compared status quo future use with a counterfactual in which all baseline users discontinued prescription sleep medication use for the rest of life. || Outcome measurements: Fall injuries serious enough to need medical treatment. In HRS this measure was available for respondents age 65 and older; ages 51–64 were imputed using NHIS data. In the simulation, fall injury was transitioned with a probit model and reported as lifetime ever incidence and average number of survey waves with any fall injury.
source_paper_title: Lifetime burden of prescription medication for insomnia in middle-aged and older adults in the US: a microsimulation study.

research_question: How might genetic propensity for body size relate to obesity in later life?
explanation: Exposure — BMI polygenic risk score: A polygenic risk score for body mass index among HRS respondents with DNA information in the 2006 wave. The paper treats the parental-generation PRS distribution as standardized approximately normal with mean 0 and variance 1, and uses the observed HRS relation between PRS and BMI to parameterize simulations. || Outcome — Body mass index and obesity status: Observed BMI in the 2006 HRS generation-0 sample is used as the target phenotype and as the outcome in the estimated BMI–PRS relation. The paper also classifies individuals into WHO-defined BMI categories and identifies obesity as BMI ≥ 30 for prevalence calculations.
source_paper_title: Generalized Stable Population and Agent-Based Models of phenotypic transmission in human populations, with an application to body size.

research_question: Could more positive views of aging protect everyday independence in later life?

research_question: Could overall cognitive health help predict diabetes in later life?

The paper does not distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes. || Exposure — Overall cognitive functioning: Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status-27 overall cognition score from respondent self/proxy-independent cognitive testing, combining recall, serial seven subtraction, and backward counting tasks. Per wave, the total of the three tests ranges from 0 to 27, with higher scores indicating higher cognitive function; descriptive results report the summed cognitive function score from 2012 to 2020 as out of 135.

research_question: How might education be related to blood pressure across social groups in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Educational attainment / years of schooling: Self-reported years of schooling, measured on a 0–17+ scale. Race and ethnicity were combined into four categories: non-Hispanic Black, non-Hispanic White, Hispanic, and non-Hispanic other race/ethnicity. research_question: Could long-term patterns of pain contribute to insomnia in later life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: At each HRS wave from 2010 through 2018, self-reported pain was coded from 0 to 3 using two pain questions: no frequent pain coded 0; if often troubled with pain, pain severity coded mild = 1, moderate = 2, severe = 3. For each item, responses of “most of the time” or “sometimes” were coded 1, and “rarely or never” was coded 0. The total JSS-4 score ranged from 0 to 4, with higher values indicating more severe insomnia problems; the four item-level symptoms were also used as network nodes.

research_question: Could sustained physical activity help protect different aspects of cognitive health in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Cumulative physical activity: Self-reported vigorous, moderate, and light/mild physical activity frequencies were coded from 0 to 4, weighted by intensity-specific MET-like weights (light=1.2, moderate=1.4, vigorous=1.8), and summed to form total MET-PA with range 0–17.6. Cumulative physical activity was then calculated as area under the curve using the trapezoid rule across repeated biennial visits, producing accumulation measures over 2-, 4-, 6-, and 8-year periods. || Outcome — Cognitive function and cognitive decline: Cognitive function was measured with the TICS-m cognitive battery. Global cognition was a 0–27 score summing memory and executive function domains. Memory combined immediate word recall (0–10) and delayed word recall (0–10). Executive function combined serial 7 subtraction (0–5) and backward counting (0–2). Higher scores indicated better cognition. Domain z-scores were calculated, and global cognition z-score was re-standardized as the mean of the two domain z-scores using 2004 baseline mean and SD for all subsequent years. Decline was assessed as longitudinal change in global cognition, memory, and executive function z-scores from 2004 through 2020.
source_paper_title: Long-term cumulative physical activity associated with less cognitive decline: Evidence from a 16-year cohort study.

Primary comparisons contrasted minoritized participants—non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic participants combined—with non-Hispanic white participants as the reference group; analyses also separately compared non-Hispanic Black vs non-Hispanic white and Hispanic vs non-Hispanic white. The same racialized categories were also used to examine effect modification of the CRP–incident dementia association. || Mediator — Systemic inflammation measured by C-reactive protein: Circulating C-reactive protein was measured from dried blood spots using ELISA. For the primary analysis, CRP was dichotomized at the 75th percentile of the analytic distribution: high systemic inflammation was defined as CRP concentration ≥4.73 μg/mL, versus lower CRP. The paper reports assay lower limit of detection as 0.035 mg/L, within-assay imprecision 8.1%, and between-assay imprecision 11.0%. || Outcome — Six-year incident dementia: Cognitive status was assessed at baseline and every two years using Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status items. The dementia classification used the Langa-Weir approach based on a subset of TICS assessments: immediate word recall, delayed word recall, serial 7s, and backward counting, scored 0–27. Scores of 0–6 were classified as dementia, 7–11 as cognitive impairment non-dementia, and 12–27 as cognitively normal. Incident dementia was defined as developing dementia during the 6-year follow-up among participants without dementia at baseline.
source_paper_title: The mediating role of systemic inflammation and moderating role of racialization in disparities in incident dementia

research_question: How do telemedicine use and willingness to use telemedicine differ across racial and ethnic groups in later life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Participant-level self-reported race and ethnicity categorized as non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black/African American, Hispanic, and other races. || Outcome — Current telemedicine use during the pandemic: Binary indicator of whether the respondent reported any telephone or video visit with a doctor instead of an in-person visit since March 2020. Responses of yes were categorized as telemedicine users; no as non-users. || Outcome — Future-intended telemedicine use: Respondents were asked how likely they were to use telephone or video doctor visits in the future. Four response options were dichotomized: very likely or somewhat likely = likely to use; not very likely or not at all likely = not likely to use.
source_paper_title: Higher than expected telemedicine use by racial and ethnic minority and cognitively impaired Medicare beneficiaries.

research_question: How might prior incarceration shape patterns of dental care use in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Prior incarceration history: Binary lifetime history of incarceration, measured from the 2012 or 2014 HRS leave-behind questionnaire. Respondents were classified as ever incarcerated versus never incarcerated based on whether they had ever been an inmate in jail, prison, juvenile detention center, or another correctional facility. || Outcome — Dental care use trajectories: Repeated binary reports of dental care use across HRS waves from 2012 through 2020, based on whether the respondent had seen a dentist for dental care, including dentures, in the last two years. These repeated yes/no measures were modeled as latent dental care trajectory groups over ages 55–90, labeled Regular Dental Care, Moderate-Declining Dental Care Use, and Low Dental Care.
source_paper_title: Dental care trajectories among formerly incarcerated older adults in the United States.

research_question: How do older adults differ in how they report the severity of health problems across domains?
explanation: Outcome measurements: In the 2007 HRS mail questionnaire, respondents rated their own health problems in six domains on a 5-point severity scale where 1=None, 2=Mild, 3=Moderate, 4=Severe, and 5=Extreme. The six domains were feeling sad/low/depressed, difficulty sleeping, difficulty concentrating or remembering things, problem moving around, shortness of breath, and pain or bodily aches. The paper excluded the work-limitation item from analysis because many respondents were no longer working. || Mediator measurements: In the 2007 HRS mail questionnaire, respondents rated 18 fictional health vignettes corresponding to the same six health domains as the self-ratings. There were three vignettes per domain, with different levels of described severity. Respondents used the same 5-point severity scale as for self-rated health: None, Mild, Moderate, Severe, Extreme. Two questionnaire versions varied by vignette-character gender and vignette order. These vignette ratings were used to estimate reporting heterogeneity / severity thresholds in CHOPIT models.
source_paper_title: Reporting heterogeneity in the associations between personality and health problems: Anchoring self-reports with health vignettes

research_question: How do race and sex shape memory performance and decline in later life?
hrs_column_ids: R3IMRC; R4IMRC; R5IMRC; R6IMRC; R7IMRC; R8IMRC; R9IMRC; R10IMRC; R11IMRC; R12IMRC; R13IMRC; R14IMRCP; R14IMRCW; R15IMRCP; R15IMRCW; R3DLRC; R4DLRC; R5DLRC; R6DLRC; R7DLRC; R8DLRC; R9DLRC; R10DLRC; R11DLRC; R12DLRC; R13DLRC; R14DLRCP; R14DLRCW; R15DLRCP; R15DLRCW; SEX; RACE; HISPANIC
explanation: Outcome measurements: Repeated late-life memory composite in HRS based on immediate and delayed recall trials of the CERAD 10-item word list memory test, using RAND-provided HRS cognitive scores including imputed cognitive scores for respondents who participated in a wave but lacked cognitive data. Composite memory scores were computed from z-scored recall variables and modeled as baseline memory performance and rate of memory decline across visits. || Moderator — Sex/gender: Participant self-report as male or female; used to compare associations between structural sexism and memory trajectories among women versus men. The authors describe the construct as sex/gender because the questionnaire wording does not clarify whether respondents reported sex or gender. || Moderator measurements: Participant identification with racialized group using 1990 U.S. Census-style categories, combined with Hispanic/Latino identification to restrict or classify participants as non-Latinx Black or non-Latinx White. Used to test whether structural-sexism associations differed between Black and White participants, particularly among women.
source_paper_title: Early life exposure to structural sexism and late-life memory trajectories among black and white women and men in the United States.

research_question: Could oral health and dental care be related to self-rated health in later life?
explanation: Outcome — Self-rated overall health: Single self-report item in the 2018 HRS asking respondents to rate their health on a 5-point scale; dichotomized as Excellent/Very Good/Good versus Fair/Poor, with Fair/Poor treated as unfavorable self-rated health. || Exposure — Dentate status / complete tooth loss: Self-reported HRS Core item identifying whether the respondent had lost all upper and lower natural permanent teeth; used to classify respondents as edentulous versus dentate. || Exposure — Recent dental care use: Self-reported HRS Core item asking whether the respondent had seen a dentist for dental care, including dentures, in the last two years; analyzed as recent dentist contact versus no recent dentist contact.
source_paper_title: A Comparative Analysis of Oral Health and Self-Rated Health: 'All of Us Research Program' vs. 'Health and Retirement Study'

research_question: How might physical activity and loneliness influence one another over time in later life?
explanation: Outcome — Loneliness: Repeated binary loneliness measure. The paper used a single CES-D-adapted item asking whether, much of the time during the past week, the respondent felt lonely, with yes/no responses. In the longitudinal models, loneliness at one wave was used both as a predictor of future loneliness/physical activity and as a future outcome predicted by prior physical activity and loneliness. || Outcome — Vigorous-intensity physical activity: Repeated binary indicator for at least weekly participation in vigorous-intensity sports or activities. Respondents were asked how often they took part in vigorous sports or activities, with examples such as running or jogging. Response categories were every day, more than once per week, once per week, one to three times per month, and never; the authors dichotomized responses into at least weekly participation versus less than weekly. In the longitudinal models, vigorous physical activity at one wave was used both as a predictor and as a future outcome. || Outcome — Moderate-intensity physical activity: Repeated binary indicator for at least weekly participation in moderately energetic sports or activities. Respondents were asked how often they took part in moderately energetic sports or activities, with examples such as walking at a moderate pace or dancing. Response categories were every day, more than once per week, once per week, one to three times per month, and never; the authors dichotomized responses into at least weekly participation versus less than weekly. In the longitudinal models, moderate physical activity at one wave was used both as a predictor and as a future outcome. Light-intensity activity was explicitly excluded from the analysis.
source_paper_title: Exercise to socialize? Bidirectional relationships between physical activity and loneliness in middle-aged and older American adults.

research_question: Do men and women differ in how consistently they report loneliness across survey formats over time?
explanation: Exposure — Interview-based loneliness status and duration: Self-reported loneliness status, yes versus no, measured biennially from 1996 through 2004 using the loneliness item from the CES-D Scale administered in HRS interviews. Loneliness duration over 1996-2004 was counted across waves and categorized as never, 1 time point, 2 time points, and ≥3 time points; analyses also coded duration continuously from 0 to 3. || Exposure — Private questionnaire UCLA loneliness scale for validation of underreporting: Self-reported 3-item UCLA Loneliness Scale from the 2006 HRS Psychosocial and Lifestyle Questionnaire, used as the best-available reference measure for loneliness in the validation study informing sensitivity and specificity of the CES-D loneliness item. Scale ranges from 3 to 9, with higher scores indicating more loneliness; cutoff ≥6 identifies individuals high in loneliness. || Moderator — Gender: Gender used to stratify models and to test effect modification of the association between loneliness duration and rate of memory decline; analyses compare men and women and use a three-way interaction among loneliness duration, years of follow-up, and gender.
source_paper_title: Could differential under-reporting of loneliness between men and women bias the gender-specific association between loneliness duration and rate of memory decline? A probabilistic bias analysis of effect modification.

research_question: Could gum treatment be related to cognitive decline in later life?
hrs_column_ids: LV508; R9COG27; R10COG27; R11COG27; R12COG27; R13COG27; R14COG27; R15COG27
explanation: Exposure — Gum treatment: At 2008 baseline, classify respondents according to whether they reported having seen a dentist or other dental provider for gum treatment since the last interview or in the last 2 years. Binary exposure: 1 = had gum treatment; 0 = no gum treatment. || Outcome — Cognitive function score / cognitive decline: Use repeated HRS cognitive function scores from the researcher-contributed cognitive dataset. Cognitive function was assessed with the Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (TICS), summing immediate and delayed recall, serial 7 subtraction, and backward counting for a total score from 0 to 27 points; higher scores indicate better cognitive functioning. Cognitive decline was modeled as change in this score over follow-up.
source_paper_title: Association of gum treatment with cognitive decline and dementia risk among older adults with periodontal symptoms: a 12-year prospective cohort study.

research_question: Could poor or worsening sleep quality increase osteoporosis risk in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Baseline sleep quality: In the HRS cohort, baseline sleep quality was measured from four sleep-disturbance items in the physical health section. Each item was scored rarely/never = 1, sometimes = 2, most of the time = 3. Scores were summed across the four items for a total range of 4–12. The paper analyzed the total score continuously and also dichotomized it as good sleep quality for scores 4–8 and poor sleep quality for scores 9–12. || Exposure — Sleep quality change trajectory: Sleep quality status was classified as good or poor at baseline and at the final sleep assessment using the HRS summed sleep-quality score cut points. Participants were categorized by change in sleep quality classification between baseline and final assessment: maintained/no change, improved from poor to good, or worsened from good to poor. The results further distinguish stable good sleep and persistently poor sleep within the maintained/no-change category. || Outcome — Incident osteoporosis: Osteoporosis was assessed by self-reported physician diagnosis during structured interviews. Respondents answering yes to ever having been diagnosed with osteoporosis by a physician were classified as having osteoporosis. For the incident outcome, participants with osteoporosis at baseline were excluded, and new diagnoses reported during follow-up from HRS Wave 12 through Wave 15 were treated as incident osteoporosis cases.
source_paper_title: Trajectories and Osteoporosis Incidence: Findings from Two Prospective Cohort Studies

research_question: Could blood-based immune profiles reflect chronic disease burden and self-rated health in later life?
hrs_column_ids: PTCELL_PCT; PBCELL_PCT; PCD4T_PCT; PCD8T_PCT; PCD4N_PCT; PCD4M_PCT; PCD4TEM_PCT; PCD4TEMRA_PCT; PCD8N_PCT; PCD8M_PCT; PCD8TEM_PCT; PCD8TEMRA_PCT; PNAIVEB_PCT; PIGD_PLUS_MEMB_PCT; PIGD_MINUS_MEMB_PCT; PC005; PC010; PC018; PC030; PC036; PC053; PC065; PC070; PC001
explanation: Exposure — Lymphocyte subset composition from blood immunophenotyping; Derived lymphocyte logratio balance measures: HRS venous blood immunophenotyping measured T- and B-cell subset percentages within the live lymphocyte gate after removing doublets. Percentages were relative to parent populations, then converted through a hierarchical tree into compositional proportions relative to total lymphocytes. The analysis used the 16 most granular lymphocyte subset proportions, including HRS-measured subsets and added “other” categories needed so lower-level cells summed to their parent populations. || Outcome — Chronic disease index: Count of self-reported doctor-diagnosed chronic conditions at the time of 2016 data collection. The index ranges from 0 to 8, summing affirmative responses for hypertension/high blood pressure, diabetes/high blood sugar, cancer or malignant tumor except skin cancer, chronic lung disease except asthma such as chronic bronchitis or emphysema, heart attack/coronary heart disease/angina/congestive heart failure/other heart problems, stroke or transient ischemic attack, emotional/nervous/psychiatric problems, and arthritis or rheumatism. Higher values indicate worse health. || Outcome — Self-reported health: Participant rating of overall health status on a five-point ordered scale from 1 = excellent to 5 = poor. Higher values indicate worse health.
source_paper_title: Compositional analysis of lymphocytes and their relationship with health outcomes: findings from the health and retirement study.

research_question: How do cognitive decline and dementia risk differ across racial and ethnic groups in later life?
hrs_column_ids: KB028; LB028; KB089M1M; LB089M1M; KB089M2M; LB089M2M; KB089M3M; LB089M3M; KB089M4M; LB089M4M; KB091M; LB091M; R8COG27; R9COG27; R10COG27; R11COG27; R12COG27; R13COG27
explanation: Exposure — Race or ethnicity: Baseline demographic race/ethnicity categorized as non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, and Hispanic. Participants with unclear race or ethnicity were excluded from the analytic sample. || Outcome — Incident dementia: Incident dementia during follow-up was defined from the modified Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status cognitive composite. The composite summed immediate word recall 0–10, delayed word recall 0–10, serial 7’s 0–5, and backward counting 0–2, for a total 0–27. Participants scoring 0–6 in the earliest follow-up wave were classified as incident dementia cases; those scoring 7 or higher throughout follow-up were classified as not having incident dementia. || Outcome — Longitudinal cognitive function / cognitive decline: Continuous modified TICS cognitive composite measured repeatedly from baseline through follow-up to estimate temporal cognitive decline. The score consisted of immediate word recall 0–10, delayed word recall 0–10, serial 7’s 0–5, and backward counting 0–2, total range 0–27.
source_paper_title: A Polysocial Approach in Exploring Racial and Ethnic Differences in Dementia and Cognitive Decline Among U.S. Older Adults: Health and Retirement Study.

research_question: Could neighborhood disorder contribute to hopelessness in later life?
hrs_column_ids: OLB020B; PLB020B; OLB020D; PLB020D; OLB020F; PLB020F; OLB020H; PLB020H; OLB018G; PLB018G; OLB018H; PLB018H; OLB018I; PLB018I; OLB018J; PLB018J
explanation: Mediator measurements: Four-item perceived neighborhood disorder scale from respondent reports in the HRS Psychological and Lifestyle Self-Administered Questionnaire, referring to the area within a 20-minute walk or about a mile from the respondent’s home. Each item was rated on a 7-point agreement scale from 1 = least agree to 7 = most strongly agree. The authors averaged responses to create a score from 1 to 7, coded the score missing if two or more items were missing, and interpreted higher scores as greater perceived disorder. || Outcome measurements: Four-item hopelessness scale from the HRS Psychological and Lifestyle Self-Administered Questionnaire in the 2014/2016 SAQ panel. Each item was rated on a 6-point Likert scale from 1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree. The authors averaged item responses to create a mean hopelessness score from 1 to 6, coded the score missing if two or more items were missing, and interpreted higher scores as greater hopelessness.
source_paper_title: Neighborhood poverty and hopelessness in older adults: The mediating role of perceived neighborhood disorder.

research_question: Could early-life exposure to sugar rationing affect heart health in later life?
hrs_column_ids: BIRTHYR; BIRTHMO; F1156A; G1289; HC036; JC036; KC036; LC036; MC036; NC036; OC036
explanation: Exposure — Pseudo early-life sugar-rationing exposure / birth-period group: Participants were grouped by date of birth according to the UK sugar-rationing natural-experiment timeline, distinguishing those whose first 1000 days after conception would have overlapped rationing from those born after rationing ended. In the HRS this is a negative-control, birth-period-based pseudo-exposure because US participants did not actually experience the UK rationing policy. The paper reports using a simplified rationed versus not rationed or birth-period comparison for HRS validation/control analyses, but the exact HRS cut points are not fully reproduced in the supplied text and are referred to figure 1/Gracner et al. || Outcome — Self-reported doctor-diagnosed heart problems: Broad longitudinal heart-problem outcome in HRS based on whether the respondent had ever had any heart condition diagnosed by a doctor. Outcomes were identified through biennial surveys, with follow-up beginning at HRS wave 4 baseline and ending when heart problems were reported, death, loss to follow-up, or study completion occurred.
source_paper_title: Exposure to sugar rationing in first 1000 days after conception and long term cardiovascular outcomes: natural experiment study.

research_question: How might long-term patterns of material hardship shape mental and physical health in later life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Multi-channel sequence exposure built from five hardship domains measured across the 2010, 2014, and 2018 HRS waves: difficulty paying bills, food insecurity, medication cutbacks because of cost, ongoing financial strain, and unaffordable housing. Individual sequences across these domains were compared using Dynamic Hamming distances and classified using Ward hierarchical clustering into five material hardship trajectory groups: least materially burdened, multiply burdened, financially burdened, housing cost burdened, and financial & housing cost burdened. || Outcome — Depressive symptoms — 8-item CES-D raw inputs, 2018: Mental health outcome measured in 2018 using the 8-item CES-D subset. Respondents answered yes/no to eight depressive-symptom/positive-affect items; positive items were reverse coded and summed to a score from 0 to 8, with higher scores indicating more depressive symptoms. || Outcome — Self-rated health, 2018: Physical health outcome measured in 2018 as a single self-rated health item on a five-point scale coded from excellent = 1 to very poor = 5, with higher values representing worse self-rated health.
source_paper_title: The association between material hardship and physical and mental health among older adults: Multi-channel sequence Approach.

research_question: Could lifelong religious and spiritual involvement shape physical functioning and depressive symptoms in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Life-course multidimensional religiosity pattern: Latent-class exposure derived from six dichotomized religiosity indicators in the 2016 HRS religious life histories experimental module: childhood and later-adulthood religious service attendance, childhood and current religious identity, and childhood and current spiritual identity. Attendance at least once per week was coded as regular; less frequent attendance was coded as infrequent. Respondents who considered themselves moderately or very religious/spiritual were coded as having stronger identity; others were coded as weaker identity. LCA assigned respondents to seven religiosity classes based on these indicators. || Outcome — Activities of daily living disability: Physical health outcome measured with the Katz Index of Independence in Activities of Daily Living. Respondents reporting difficulty with one or more of six activities were coded as having a disability. The paper assessed disability at 2016 baseline and replicated the measure in 2018 for two-year follow-up analyses. || Outcome — Probable depression based on depressive symptoms: Psychological health outcome measured using eight CES-D items asking about experiences over the past week. The happy and joy-in-life items were reverse coded. Respondents with depressive symptomology on three or more items were categorized as having probable depression. The paper assessed probable depression at 2016 baseline and replicated the measure in 2018 for two-year follow-up analyses.
source_paper_title: Linking Multi-Dimensional Religiosity in Childhood and Later Adulthood: Implications for Later Life Health.

research_question: Could education help protect verbal memory over time in later life?
hrs_column_ids: R11DLRC; R13DLRC; R14DLRCP; R14DLRCW; R15DLRCP; R15DLRCW; NZ216
explanation: Outcome — Verbal memory trajectory: Delayed word-list recall score observed longitudinally, using one round of word recall in each study. Participants were randomly assigned one of two word lists; the list had 10 words in HRS and CHARLS and 8 words in MHAS. The paper used the delayed recall measure as verbal memory, standardized within each database to a baseline-centered z-score: baseline scores were converted using the baseline sample mean and standard deviation, and follow-up scores were converted using those same baseline metrics. || Exposure — Educational attainment: Highest degree attained, coded as a six-category ordinal measure: no education, some elementary school, elementary school, middle school, high school, and college or professional degree. High school education was used as the reference category in models because education distributions differed across databases.
source_paper_title: Education and age of decline in verbal memory across countries: Evidence from the HRS, MHAS, and CHARLS.

research_question: Could the timing and severity of head injuries shape memory in later life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Retrospective 2014 HRS experimental module asking whether respondents had ever experienced different types of head or neck injuries. The primary analyses focused on three injury causes with larger sample sizes: vehicle accident; fall or being hit by something; and sports or playground injury. For each endorsed injury type, respondents reported age when the injury occurred, in years, and whether they were dazed or had a gap in memory; memory gap was coded dichotomously as no/yes. Age of onset was grand-mean-centered separately by TBI type for modeling, but the construct is the reported age at injury. || Outcome — Self-rated memory: Single self-report item at survey completion rating present memory on a 5-point scale from poor to excellent, coded 0 to 4 with higher values indicating better memory. || Outcome measurements: Recall task in which respondents listed as many words as they could remember from a 10-word list immediately and after a delay. The paper analyzed combined recall performance as a word count, with higher values indicating better cognitive health.
source_paper_title: Associations Between Traumatic Brain Injury Characteristics and Memory Outcomes: Insights from the Health and Retirement Study

research_question: Could sleep problems help predict mild cognitive impairment in later life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Three individual baseline self-reported sleep disturbance items from the adapted Jenkins Sleep Scale were assessed in 2018: trouble falling asleep, trouble waking up during the night, and waking too early and being unable to fall asleep again. Each item used response categories of most of the time, sometimes, or rarely/never; the paper analyzed the items separately rather than as a composite scale. || Outcome measurements: Follow-up cognitive status in 2020 was derived from objective HRS cognitive tests. Immediate word recall, delayed word recall, serial 7s, and backward counting from 20 were summed to a total cognitive score ranging from 0 to 27. Using Lang-Weir cut points, 12–27 indicated no cognitive impairment, 7–11 indicated cognitive impairment without dementia/MCI without dementia, and 0–6 indicated dementia. The focal binary outcome was MCI without dementia versus no MCI among those not classified as having dementia.
source_paper_title: Association of reported sleep disturbances with objectively assessed mild cognitive impairment among adults in the United States.

research_question: Could digital exclusion contribute to depressive symptoms in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Digital exclusion / internet non-use: Self-reported regular internet use in HRS. Respondents were classified as digitally excluded if they answered “no” to regularly using the Internet/World Wide Web for email or other purposes; digital inclusion if they answered “yes.”. || Outcome — Depressive symptoms: Eight-item CES-D depressive symptom score in HRS, based on yes/no symptom items from the past week. The two positive-affect items were reverse coded. Total score ranged from 0 to 8; participants scoring 3 or higher were coded as having depressive symptoms, otherwise as not having depressive symptoms.
source_paper_title: Digital Exclusion and Depressive Symptoms among Older People: Findings from Five Aging Cohort Studies across 24 Countries.

research_question: Could education and volunteering help protect cognitive health over time?
explanation: Outcome — Total cognitive function trajectory: Repeated total cognitive function score from HRS cognitive testing, analyzed longitudinally from 2006 through 2020 as a growth trajectory over age. The paper refers to the Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status / modified TICS and describes a 27-point cognitive measure, with higher scores indicating better cognition; baseline normal cognitive health required scores above the dementia cutpoint (>6). Exact component items of the total score are not fully visible in the supplied text. || Exposure — Educational attainment: Highest educational attainment categorized as less than high school, high school degree, some college, or college degree or more; modeled with less than high school as the lowest category and higher categories compared in growth models. || Exposure measurements: Two volunteering measures based on hours in the previous year. Formal volunteering captured hours volunteered for religious, educational, health-related, or other charitable organizations. Informal volunteering captured hours spent helping friends, neighbors, or relatives who did not live with the respondent and did not pay for the help. Each type was categorized as no volunteering, less than 100 hours, or 100 or more hours in the previous year.
source_paper_title: Modifiable factors associated with cognitive health trajectories among Indigenous, Hispanic, Black, and White older adults: an exploratory longitudinal panel analysis of the health and retirement study with a focus on Indigenous peoples.

research_question: Could physical activity encourage mammography screening among older women, and does race or ethnicity matter?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Main exposure was a physical activity index derived from self-reported frequency of light, moderate, and vigorous activities. Each intensity item used five response options from every day to never. Responses were assigned intensity-specific scores, summed to an index with possible range 0–54, and dichotomized as inactive if the score was below 21 versus active otherwise. The paper describes using lagged physical activity as the main exposure so that activity preceded mammography screening. || Outcome — Mammography screening utilization: Self-reported mammography screening use, coded binary yes/no. Women were asked whether they had a mammogram or X-ray of the breast to search for cancer in the last two years or, in later waves, since the previous wave. The paper’s primary longitudinal description focuses on follow-up mammography screening after the physical activity baseline, especially waves 9, 11, and 13 corresponding to 2008, 2012, and 2016, though the measures section also mentions assessment from wave 8 through wave 13. || Moderator — Race/ethnicity: Race/ethnicity was categorized into three groups for adjustment and effect modification: non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, and Hispanic. The study tested whether the association between physical activity and mammography screening differed across these groups.
source_paper_title: The association between physical activity and mammography screening utilization: a longitudinal analysis, health retirement study (2004-2016).

research_question: Does cognitive impairment differ across racial and ethnic groups in later life?
hrs_column_ids: R4COG27; R5COG27; R6COG27; R7COG27; R8COG27; R9COG27; R10COG27; R11COG27; R12COG27; R13COG27; R14COG27; R15COG27; RACE; HISPANIC
explanation: Exposure — Cognitive impairment with likely dementia - 27-point modified TICS score: Cognitive function was measured at each study wave using a 27-point modified Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status score summing immediate recall, delayed recall, backwards counting, and serial sevens. Respondents with TICS score below 7 were categorized as cognitively impaired with likely dementia. Treated as a time-varying chronic-condition indicator in the mortality contribution analyses. || Moderator — Race and ethnicity group: Respondents were classified into three mutually exclusive racial/ethnic groups used for stratified mortality models and LE-AAF estimates: non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, and Hispanic. Respondents missing race/ethnicity or reporting an “other” non-Hispanic category were excluded from the analytic sample.
source_paper_title: Contribution of chronic conditions to mortality: Differences by race and ethnicity

research_question: Could complete tooth loss undermine healthy aging in later life?
explanation: Exposure — Tooth loss / edentulism: Binary tooth-loss status from the 2012 HRS tooth loss question, analyzed as complete tooth loss / edentulism versus being dentate. The exact question wording and coding are not provided in the supplied text. || Outcome measurements: Aggregate binary healthy ageing measure at final follow-up. Participants were classified as healthy only if they were free from cognitive impairment, free from disability, and had high physical functioning; otherwise they were classified as not healthy. Cognitive impairment threshold: score ≥12 out of 27 on immediate and delayed word recall, serial subtraction, and backwards counting. Freedom from disability: no difficulty with 6 ADLs and 5 IADLs. High physical functioning: ≤1 difficulty among 11 physical-functioning tasks. Coding reported as 0 = healthy if all three domains healthy, 1 = not healthy.
source_paper_title: The Nutritional Pathway Between Tooth Loss and Healthy Ageing: A Longitudinal Study of Older American Adults.

research_question: Does exercising in later life predict whether older adults remain physically active over time?
explanation: Exposure — Baseline participation in at least some moderate or vigorous exercise: At the baseline predictor wave, exercise behavior was based on HRS vigorous-activity and moderate-activity frequency items referring to the past 12 months. For each intensity, response options were daily, more than once per week, once per week, one to three times per month, or never. Participants were classified as doing at least some exercise if they reported either vigorous or moderate activity at any frequency from daily through one to three times per month; otherwise they were classified as never exercising. || Outcome — Follow-up participation in at least some moderate or vigorous exercise: At the outcome wave, exercise behavior was measured with the same HRS vigorous-activity and moderate-activity frequency items for the past 12 months. The paper dichotomized responses into never exercising versus any reported vigorous or moderate activity, where any frequency from daily to one to three times per month on either intensity counted as “at least some” exercise. No duration measure was available.
source_paper_title: Exploring novel determinants of exercise behavior: a lagged exposure-wide approach.

research_question: Could central obesity increase the risk of developing depressive symptoms in later life?
explanation: Exposure measurements: Calculated at baseline as waist circumference in centimeters divided by the square root of body weight in kilograms. The paper analyzed WWI both continuously per unit increase and in quartiles. For HRS, baseline was Wave 8, 2006–2007; waist was measured at the navel and recorded to the nearest quarter inch, and net weight was measured using a portable electronic scale. || Outcome measurements: Depressive symptoms were assessed biennially during follow-up with the 8-item Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale. Participants reported whether each symptom occurred in the preceding week, with yes/no responses summed from 0 to 8 after scoring yes = 1 and no = 0. A CESD-8 score of 3 or higher was used to identify notable depressive symptoms. For HRS, follow-up was Waves 9 through 15 after Wave 8 baseline.

research_question: Could instability in resting heart rate over time be related to cognitive decline in later life?

The main exposure was variability independent of the mean (VIM), calculated as 100 × SD / mean^beta, where beta is from the regression of ln(SD) on ln(mean). Higher VIM indicates greater visit-to-visit resting heart-rate variability. CV and ARV were calculated only for sensitivity analyses. || Outcome — Cognitive functioning over repeated visits: Cognitive function was measured biennially at each wave using questionnaire-based tests covering memory, orientation, and executive function. The paper defined global cognitive function as the sum of scores across memory, orientation, and executive-function dimensions and analyzed global and domain-specific cognitive function as z scores.
